entries.modern_form: PIE *bʰer- 'to bear, carry' (Pokorny 128, Watkins bher-1) and PIE *bʰréh₂tēr 'brother' (Pokorny 163, Watkins bhrater-) — two separate roots in every modern handbook
entries.note: Both halves of the box are real and the language label and glosses are right: Pokorny p. 128 has '1. bher- ,tragen, bringen‘ usw. (auch Leibesfrucht tragen; med. ,ferri‘), auch ,aufheben, erheben‘' and p. 163 has 'bhrāter- ,Angehöriger der Großfamilie, Bruder, Blutsverwandter‘'. Buck p. 107 §2.44 and Watkins confirm both. What is Nourai's own and NOT supported is the analytical gloss that ties them together — 'Bhrâ-tar: load carrier (of family)'. No standard authority derives *bʰréh₂tēr from *bʰer-: Pokorny gives them as two independent lemmas 35 pages apart, Watkins gives them two separate root entries, and Wiktionary/Beekes treat *bʰréh₂tēr as an unanalysable primary kinship term of the *-h₂ter class (like *ph₂tēr, *méh₂tēr, *dʰugh₂tēr), with the same suffix as those but no verbal root. Watkins's essay in the appendix (line 155) says only 'Male blood relations were designated as bhrater- (BROTHER), which doubtless extended beyond those with a common father or mother'. The similarity bhrā- : bher- is accidental. Everything below the box is nevertheless correct, because Nourai has drawn the two families side by side rather than one out of the other. Nourai's cross-reference '☞ Ter 3' (the -ter kinship suffix) shows he was aware of the suffix analysis.
entries.note_fa: هر دو ریشهٔ داخل کادر واقعی‌اند و برچسب زبانی و معنا درست است: پوکورنی در صفحهٔ ۱۲۸ ریشهٔ *bʰer- «بردن، آوردن» و در صفحهٔ ۱۶۳ ریشهٔ *bʰrāter- «برادر، خویشاوند نزدیک» را جداگانه آورده است. آنچه از آنِ نورایی است و پشتیبانی ندارد، تفسیر «برادر = باربرِ خانواده» است؛ هیچ مرجع معتبری *bʰréh₂tēr را از *bʰer- نمی‌گیرد. ریشه‌شناسی امروزی «برادر» را واژه‌ای بنیادین از خانوادهٔ نام‌های خویشاوندی با پسوند *-h₂ter (مانند پدر، مادر، دختر) می‌داند که ستاک فعلی قابل تجزیه‌ای ندارد؛ شباهت bhrā- با bher- تصادفی است. با این همه، چون نورایی دو خانواده را در کنار هم و نه یکی از دلِ دیگری رسم کرده، همهٔ شاخه‌های زیرین درست‌اند. پس ریشه با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Old Persian bar- 'to bear, carry' is well attested: 3 pl. bara⁺tiy 'they bear' (DB 5.22, DNa 42), impf. abaram/abara, imv. baratuv, inf. bartanaiy, pass. abariya (DSf). It continues PIE *bʰer-e/o- exactly as Skt. bhárati, Av. baraiti, Gk. phérō, Lat. ferō, Goth. bairþ. The second gloss 'ride a horse' is not a separate verb but the specialised Iranian use that Pokorny records for Avestan ('av. baraiti ds. und ,reiten‘') and that surfaces in the OP vr̥ddhi compounds asa-bāra- 'horse-borne' and uša-bāri- 'camel-borne' (Kent §122, §126), whence MP aswār > NP سوار savār. Nourai's box is therefore right, though 'ride' belongs to the derived bāra- stem rather than to bar- itself.

nodes.derivation: All five prefixed compounds are Kent's own list on the very page Nourai cites: ā + bar- 'perform' (ābaratiy, DNb 25); pati- + ā + bar- 'bring back, restore' (patiyābaram, DB 1.68 — a rare OP double prefix, Kent §379); parā + bar- 'bear away, take away' (parābara DB 1.71, 96; parābartam DB 1.62); pari- + bar- 'protect, preserve' (paribarāmiy DNb 17, paribarā DB 4.72, 88); fra- + bar- 'proffer, grant' (frābara, the standard Achaemenid formula '(Ahuramazdā) granted me this kingdom'). Phonetically pati-ā- contracts to patiyā- and para+ā to parā-, and pari- keeps its -i- before a consonant (Kent §1678). The Persian continuations Nourai cross-references (پروردن < pari-bar-, فراوردن/آوردن < ā-bar-) are the regular MP-NP outcomes.

nodes.derivation: Gk. φέρειν (phérein) 'to carry' is the direct thematic continuation of PIE *bʰér-e-ti, the same present as Skt. bhárati and Lat. ferō. φωσφόρος (phōsphóros) 'light-bearing, the morning star' is a possessive compound of φῶς (< *φάος, from PIE *bʰeh₂- 'to shine' — hence Nourai's cross-reference to his root Bhâ 1) and the -φόρος agent element of φέρω. So the node is right on both counts: only the second element belongs to Bher, the first to Bhā.

nodes.derivation: French phosphore is the 18th-century learned formation on Modern Latin phosphorus, the name given to the substance Hennig Brand isolated from urine at Hamburg in 1669 because it glowed in the dark; Lavoisier proved it an element in 1777, and by then phosphore was the settled French chemical term (Etymonline: 'phosphate (1795), from French phosphate, from phosphore'). The word therefore reaches French through Latin rather than straight from Greek, but the Greek etymon in Nourai's box is right.

nodes.derivation: The word itself belongs to this root, but the arrow as drawn is wrong. English phosphor is first recorded in the 1630s meaning 'the morning star, Lucifer', taken straight from Latin Phosphorus < Gk. φωσφόρος, and its sense 'anything phosphorescent' is 1705; the chemical name phosphorus is Modern Latin of the 1670s. All of this is earlier than, and independent of, French phosphore. Klein: 'phosphorus, n. — ModL. phosphorus, fr. L. Phosphorus, ... fr. Gk. φωσφόρος' — no French link; Etymonline agrees. French is the immediate source of Persian فسفر (node #5) but not of the English word, so the branch French > English should be Latin/Greek > English. The ultimate etymology in Nourai's chart is nonetheless correct.

nodes.derivation: Lat. ferō, ferre 'to carry' is the athematic/thematic present of *bʰer-, with the regular Italic change of word-initial *bʰ to f- (contrast Greek ph- and Germanic b-); its suppletive perfect tulī and participle lātus come from a different root (*telh₂-). nodes.derivation: All eight verbs are Latin preverb + ferre borrowed into English through Old French or directly from Latin: dē-ferō > deferre 'carry away, submit', dis-ferō > differre 'carry apart', ob-ferō > offerre 'bring before', prae-ferō, re-ferō, sub-ferō > sufferre, trāns-ferō; fertile is L. fertilis 'bearing (crops)', an -ilis adjective on the same stem. nodes.derivation: The reconstruction is genuinely Mann's, on the column Nourai cites: 'ambhor-, ambhr- (for ambh-bhor, -bhr-, cf. ambhō and bher-, bhor-) „two-handled vessel‘'. So the segmentation *ambh(i)- 'on both sides' + the o-grade *bʰor-o- 'carrier' is Mann's, and the Greek witness ἀμφορεύς / ἀμφιφορεύς (> Lat. amphora) is uncontroversial. But two things differ from the chart: Mann's gloss is 'two-handled VESSEL', not 'a two-handled tool for carrying (hot) objects' (Nourai has silently substituted the Persian sense of انبر), and no other authority reconstructs a PIE noun here — Pokorny and Watkins treat ἀμφορεύς as an inner-Greek compound of ἀμφί + φέρω (Watkins files AMPHORA under bher-1 §8, i.e. Greek), and OE amber / OHG ampri are usually taken as loans from Latin amphora rather than as inherited cognates. The node is therefore correctly reported from Mann but rests on a single, minority reconstruction.

nodes.derivation: NP انبر anbor/ambor 'tongs, pliers' (with انبره and the compound انبردست 'pliers') is a real and old Persian word — Dehkhoda and Moʾin define it as 'آلت فلزی دوشاخه که با آن آتش یا چیز دیگر را برگیرند', which is where Nourai's gloss 'tool for carrying hot objects' comes from. The etymology, however, rests entirely on the two words 'Per. ambar' in Mann's article: no other source in the library derives it from *ambhi-bʰor-. Horn, Hübschmann, MacKenzie and Nyberg are silent (no Middle Persian *ambar 'tongs' is attested), Moʾin and Dehkhoda give no origin tag, and Wiktionary offers a quite different (and unsourced) derivation 'from Middle Iranian, from PIE *h₂eḱ- „sharp‘'. The internal Persian analysis that Persian writers usually give — ham- 'together' + -bar from بردن 'to carry' — would still land in this root but as a New Persian compound, not an inherited PIE noun. Formally *ambi-bara- > *ambar > انبر is unobjectionable (haplology of the two labials, n before b written ن but pronounced [m]); the derivation is possible but unproven.
nodes.derivation_fa: «انبر» واژه‌ای کهن و اصیل فارسی است؛ دهخدا و معین آن را «آلت فلزی دوشاخه که با آن آتش یا چیز دیگر را برگیرند» معنا کرده‌اند. اما ریشه‌شناسی آن تنها بر دو کلمهٔ «Per. ambar» در مدخل من تکیه دارد: هرن، هوبشمان، مکنزی و نیبرگ دربارهٔ آن خاموشند و هیچ صورت فارسی میانه‌ای گواه ندارد؛ معین و دهخدا نیز نشانهٔ خاستگاه نمی‌دهند، و ویکی‌واژه آن را به ریشهٔ دیگری (*h₂eḱ- «تیز») می‌برد. از نظر آوایی *ambi-bara- > *ambar > انبر (با حذف یکی از دو لبی) ممکن است، اما ثابت نیست؛ پس با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

entries.modern_form: PIE *bʰerǵ- ~ *bʰreǵ- 'to roast, fry' — Pokorny's '6. bher- mit g-Erweiterungen ... rösten, backen, kochen' (IEW 137), Watkins's bher-4 'to cook, bake'
entries.note: The page number is right and so is the meaning, but the shape of the root is not what Nourai's own reference prints. Pokorny p. 137 does not have a bare '2. bher- ‚to cook‘'; it has '6. bher- mit g-Erweiterungen, wovor z.T. i-, u-Vokale, ,rösten, backen, kochen‘; von 2. bher- ‚sich heftig bewegen, wallen, kochen‘ abgeleitet' — i.e. the root that means 'to cook' is always the g-extended one (bhereg-, bhrēi-g-, bhrūg-), and Pokorny's '2. bher-' (p. 132) means 'to well up, seethe'. Nourai has taken the page-137 meaning and Pokorny's number 2 from two different lemmas. Watkins avoids the problem by giving the entry as 'bher-4. To cook, bake. Extended root form *bhrig- in Latin frigere ... [Pok. 6. bher- 137]', and today's reconstruction is *bʰerǵ- ~ *bʰreǵ- with a zero-grade ye-present *bʰr̥ǵ-yé-ti behind Skt. bhṛjjáti, Gk. φρύγω, Lat. frīgō and Iranian *brij-/*braij-. So: right page, right sense, wrong root shape and number. Everything hanging under the box is Pokorny's own material from that page.

nodes.words: beresteh «برشته»; beryân «بریان»; berîjab «بریجب»; (extra) برشتن ؛ بریز ، بریزن
nodes.derivation: The first two words are confirmed. برشته berešte 'roasted, toasted' is the past participle of برشتن berištan (the parenthesis the book prints beside it) < MP brištan < Iranian *br̥j-ta-; بریان beryān 'roasted' is Pokorny's 'npers. biryān (*brigāna-)', and Borhan-e Qateʾ defines it 'بریان: (از مصدر برشتن) کباب‌شده، برشته‌شده، کباب'; the present stem بریز beriz that the book puts in the extras is the regular MP brēz-. The THIRD word is corrupt in two different ways. (a) The printed page shows the Persian script as «بریجَن» (final nūn, dot above, with a fatha on the jīm), not بریجب as the JSON has it — this is an EXTRACTION error, the last letter was read as bāʾ. (b) The book's own Latin transliteration 'berîjab' is itself a misprint for berījan: Borhan-e Qateʾ p. 269 has 'بریجن ... با جیم بر وزن رسیدن، تنوری باشد که در آن کماج و نان سنگک پزند، و عربی فُرن گویند' (with Moʾin's footnote 'بریجن، پهلوی ... ایرانی باستان *braij'), and Horn p. 47 gives the same word as 'berīzen, birezen ‚Backofen‘', Pokorny p. 137 as 'bᵉrezan ‚Backofen‘'. There is no Persian *berījab. The etymology itself is sound: *braij-ana- 'roasting place' > بریزن/بریجن, with the usual z/j fluctuation of the Iranian palatal.
nodes.derivation_fa: دو واژهٔ نخست درست‌اند: «برشته» صفت مفعولی «برشتن» است که از فارسی میانهٔ brištan می‌آید، و «بریان» همان است که پوکورنی با بازساخت *brigāna- می‌آورد و برهان قاطع آن را «(از مصدر برشتن) کباب‌شده، برشته‌شده» معنا کرده است. واژهٔ سوم دو خطا دارد: یکی خطای خوانش اسکن — در صفحهٔ چاپی «بریجَن» با نون پایانی آمده ولی در دادهٔ استخراج‌شده «بریجب» ضبط شده است؛ دیگری خطای چاپی خود کتاب — آوانویسی لاتین «berîjab» به جای berījan. برهان قاطع (ص ۲۶۹) می‌نویسد: «بریجن، با جیم، بر وزن رسیدن، تنوری باشد که در آن کماج و نان سنگک پزند»، و معین در حاشیه آن را پهلوی و از ایرانی باستان *braij می‌داند؛ هرن نیز «berīzen ‚Backofen‘» آورده است. واژه‌ای به شکل *بریجب در فارسی وجود ندارد.

nodes.derivation: Lat. frīgō, frīgere 'to roast, parch, fry' continues the i-grade of the same extended root: Watkins files it as 'bher-4. To cook, bake. Extended root form *bhrig- in Latin frigere ... [Pok. 6. bher- 137]', and Pokorny prints 'Lat. frīgō, -ere ‚rösten, dörren‘, umbr. frehtu ‚gekocht‘' immediately after the Iranian forms of Nourai's other branch. Ernout-Meillet stress that the original sense was 'faire sécher par la cuisson, cuire à sec' and that 'frire' is secondary, and compare 'gr. φρύγω ‚je fais griller‘, skr. bhrjyáti' — the same three-way i/u/zero distribution Pokorny describes.
nodes.derivation_fa: لاتین frīgō/frīgere «برشته کردن، خشک پختن» از همان ریشهٔ گسترده با واکهٔ i است: واتکینز آن را ذیل bher-4 «پختن، پوختن» با صورت گستردهٔ *bhrig- می‌آورد و پوکورنی در همان صفحهٔ ۱۳۷ بلافاصله پس از صورت‌های ایرانی می‌آورد. ارنو-میه معنای اصلی را «خشک‌پختن» می‌دانند و یونانی phrýgō و سنسکریت bhrjyáti را هم‌سنگ آن می‌آورند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: English fry is ME frien, borrowed c.1300 from Old French frire, the regular French outcome of Lat. frīgere (with the Latin infinitive remade as a 4th-conjugation *frīgīre in Vulgar Latin). Watkins ends the bher-4 entry with 'Latin frigere, to roast, fry: FRY', so the whole chain Latin > (French) > English is on record; Nourai's chart compresses the Old French stage, as he does throughout for Latin-to-English borrowings.
